Part 1 of 2 -- slides 50-60, 6 question(s): covered (confidence 0.90)

The slide set for Topic 5 (slides 50‑60) provides a comprehensive treatment of the six student questions.  The slides explicitly define VMX root and non‑root modes, describe the VMCALL instruction and the concept of hypercalls, and walk through the Intel VT‑x/AMD‑v execution model—including the duplication of privileged state, the two VMX modes, and the VM‑exit/VM‑resume cycle that KVM uses.  The rationale for widespread hardware assistance is addressed in the discussion of the challenges of x86‑64 virtualization (hiding privileged state and preventing VMs from altering system state) and the subsequent “Current status of H/W assist” slide that notes almost all VMMs rely on this feature.  Xen’s architecture slide clarifies the distinct roles of the Xen hypervisor and Dom0, while the KVM architecture slide explains how the Linux kernel is extended to act as a hypervisor, leveraging VT‑x, EPT, and kernel scheduling.  No question appears to be left unanswered or only partially addressed; all concepts are covered within the topic’s own slides or in adjacent slides that naturally belong to the same topic.  Therefore, the deck offers full coverage for these questions.  If further depth is desired, a brief note on the performance benefits of hardware assistance (e.g., reduced VM‑exit overhead) could be added to the “Current status of H/W assist” slide.

Part 2 of 2 -- slides 69-79, 7 question(s): covered (confidence 0.90)

The slide set for Topic 5 (slides 69‑79) provides a complete, coherent answer to each of the seven student questions.  Slides 69‑71 introduce the shadow page table, explain why it is needed (to give the hypervisor a direct mapping of guest virtual to host physical addresses), and describe the write‑protect mechanism that forces the hypervisor to trap any guest modification.  Slides 72‑74 detail how the hypervisor keeps the shadow page table in sync—every write to a guest page table triggers a page‑fault trap, after which the VMM updates the corresponding shadow entry.  The transition to hardware‑assisted memory virtualization is covered in slides 75‑78, where the concept of Nested/Extended Page Tables (EPT) is introduced, the two‑level translation (guest page table → EPT) is shown, and the differences from shadow paging are highlighted (no need for traps, no TLB flush on world switches).  Finally, slide 79 explicitly states that EPT improves memory‑virtualization performance by eliminating the overhead of shadow‑table maintenance and reducing VM‑exit traffic.  While the performance discussion is brief, the key points are present and directly answer the last question.  Overall, the topic’s slides adequately cover all matched questions, so the gap type is "covered".
